The sample is very small and drawn from an ICU, and the patients are children with severe disease, so the findings do not represent typical early COVID-19 symptoms such as fever, cough, fatigue, or loss of smell and taste. The paper also does not describe the order in which symptoms appeared. It offers useful related information, but it does not directly answer the question for the general population.

This Diamond Princess cohort describes clinical features of SARS-CoV-2 infection, including asymptomatic, mild and severe presentations. However, the abstract does not list the initial symptoms (such as fever, cough, or fatigue) or their order of onset. It focuses on risk factors for progression (older age, chest CT consolidation, lymphopenia, elevated LDH) and on how many people were asymptomatic. This is useful context on the clinical spectrum and early disease, but it does not directly answer the question about initial symptoms.

The document is a review of nanoparticle-based vaccines for respiratory infections and the animal models used to test them. It does not address asymptomatic COVID-19 infection, including its prevalence, transmission, or clinical features. It does not mention COVID-19 or asymptomatic carriers, so it is not relevant to the research question.

The document describes a one-step duplex PCR assay for detecting canine distemper virus and canine coronavirus in dogs. It has nothing to do with SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19 or with asymptomatic human infection. Canine coronavirus is a different virus, so the document gives no information relevant to the research question.

The study directly addresses asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection in a large cohort of 554 health care workers who were at work and asymptomatic. It reports a point prevalence of active infection (2.39%) among asymptomatic workers. It shows that asymptomatic seroconversion occurs (17.1% in those with no prior symptoms), and that antibody responses are quantitatively lower than after symptomatic illness. These findings speak to the immune response and prevalence of asymptomatic infection, which are core aspects of the question. Limitations: it is a cross-sectional design, relies on self-reported prior symptoms, and does not address transmission, viral load, or clinical outcomes of asymptomatic individuals. It therefore gives substantial but not comprehensive coverage of what is known about asymptomatic infection.

The study includes asymptomatic and mild COVID-19 patients (n=211) and identifies risk factors for progression to severe disease: initial abnormal chest X-ray, chills, fever above 37.5 °C, and diabetes. This is useful for understanding the clinical course and monitoring needs of initially asymptomatic patients. However, it does not focus solely on asymptomatic individuals. It groups them with mild cases and does not address transmission, prevalence, viral shedding, or other characteristics of asymptomatic infection. The relevance is therefore moderate.

This systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric COVID-19 reports a pooled asymptomatic proportion of 26% among children, and notes that most cases were mild and that household contact was common. That is directly relevant to the question about asymptomatic infection, but only a small part of the abstract covers it. The population is limited to children, and the abstract does not address asymptomatic transmission, viral shedding, or long-term outcomes. It is moderately useful, with quantitative evidence on asymptomatic prevalence in a specific subgroup.

This narrative review directly addresses the research question. It synthesizes evidence on asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection: the proportion of infections that are asymptomatic (about 40-45%), their ability to transmit the virus for an extended period (possibly more than 14 days), subclinical lung abnormalities on CT, and the implications for testing and surveillance. These findings cover prevalence, transmissibility, clinical features, and public health response, which are the main things known about asymptomatic infected people. Because it is a narrative review rather than a systematic review or meta-analysis, the strength of evidence is somewhat limited, but the topical match is very strong.

This document describes the lung pathology of early-phase COVID-19 pneumonia in two lung cancer patients who had lobectomies. It does not mention hydroxychloroquine, any treatment, or therapeutic outcomes, so it provides no evidence on whether hydroxychloroquine helps in COVID-19. It is not relevant to the research question.

The document is a retrospective study of myocardial injury and myocarditis in COVID-19 patients in Wuhan. It does not mention hydroxychloroquine or any treatment, so it provides no evidence on hydroxychloroquine's value. It is not relevant to the research question.

This is a general guideline for managing critically ill adults with COVID-19. The abstract says it covers 'COVID-19 therapy' among its topics, and the full guideline does address hydroxychloroquine, but the abstract never mentions the drug or presents any evidence on its value. Any hydroxychloroquine recommendation would be a small part of a broad document. The abstract itself offers little direct evidence on the question, so the document is only marginally relevant.

This study evaluates hydroxychloroquine added to pegylated interferon plus ribavirin in Egyptian patients with genotype-4 chronic hepatitis C. It says nothing about COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2, so it provides no direct evidence on HCQ for COVID-19. At most it shows HCQ has some antiviral activity and an acceptable short-term safety profile in a different viral infection, which is not enough to support any conclusion about COVID-19 treatment.

This is a pharmacokinetic modeling paper on HCQ dosing regimens in COVID-19. It does not test whether HCQ works. It touches on clinical efficacy and safety data only to contextualize the model predictions, and it notes variable clinical responses to the same fixed doses. Its claim that 80% of patients may not need doses above 800 mg on day 1 and 600 mg daily afterward assumes a therapeutic benefit that it does not establish. Its conclusion calls for better characterization of target exposures. The paper therefore says little about whether HCQ is valuable in COVID-19 and is only tangentially relevant.

This is a mechanistic review of how chloroquine/hydroxychloroquine might act against viral infections, including SARS-CoV-2. It covers the rationale for repurposing: lysosomal pH alteration, blocked endocytosis and phagolysosomal fusion, and dampening of the cytokine storm. It does not present clinical or trial evidence of HCQ efficacy in COVID-19. It states that clinical testing is still urgently needed, so it supports the theoretical case for HCQ rather than showing demonstrated value. It is therefore moderately relevant: useful background on biological plausibility, but not direct evidence of treatment benefit.

This is a general, pre-COVID review of the pathogenetic and clinical aspects of Coronaviridae, focused mainly on veterinary coronaviruses of cattle and pets. It does not cover SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-2–human protein interactions, drug targets, or drug repurposing, so it does not address the research question.

The document is about Ebola virus entry and antiviral discovery, including surrogate models, screening, and drug repurposing for EVD. It does not cover SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV-2–human protein interactions, or repurposing approved drugs for COVID-19. The only overlap is the general concept of drug repurposing for a viral infection, which is too tangential to help answer the question.

CORDITE is a curated database that aggregates data on potential drugs and drug repurposing candidates for SARS-CoV-2, so it bears on the question of repurposing approved drugs. The abstract, however, does not describe specific SARS-CoV-2–human protein interactions or identify which interactions point to druggable targets. It provides no findings, specific drugs, or evidence on interaction-based target prioritization. It is a useful resource that could help locate repurposing candidates, but it does not directly answer the question.

The document examines a specific SARS-CoV-2 protein-host component interaction: the Spike S1 RBD binding to heparin/heparan sulphate. It shows that approved anticoagulant drugs (unfractionated heparin and various low molecular weight heparins, including enoxaparin) bind the RBD and induce conformational change, and it explicitly proposes repurposing them as antivirals. This directly addresses the drug repurposing part of the question and gives a viral-host interaction that could be a target. It is not a broad interactome (protein-protein) study of human protein interactions, and it relies on biophysical binding data rather than clinical or cellular efficacy evidence. The interaction is also with a host glycosaminoglycan, not a human protein. So it is highly relevant but only partially covers the question.

The abstract is a review of drugs, both novel and repurposed, that target the SARS-CoV-2 machinery: the spike glycoprotein binding ACE2, RdRp, and the main protease (3CLpro/Mpro). It therefore partly covers the question of drug targets and repurposing. The spike-ACE2 interaction is a true virus-human protein interaction, and the abstract mentions repurposed drugs. However, it focuses mainly on viral proteins and enzymes, not on systematic SARS-CoV-2-human protein-protein interaction maps. It also names no specific approved drugs and gives no evidence in the abstract. It is moderately relevant, but it does not directly answer the question.

This JAMA review addresses drug repurposing for COVID-19 in general terms. It notes that SARS-CoV-2 virology offers many potential drug targets and discusses candidate drugs such as remdesivir, oseltamivir, corticosteroids, and ACE inhibitors/ARBs. It does not analyze SARS-CoV-2–human protein-protein interactions or use them to identify drug targets, so it only partly answers the question. It is relevant to the repurposing part, but it does not give the interaction-based evidence the question asks for. It also concludes that no therapy has proven effective.

The document is a general review of the molecular mechanisms, benefits, and risks of herbal medicine and traditional Chinese medicine, with acute airway viral infections as examples. The abstract never mentions remdesivir, antiviral drug efficacy, or COVID-19 treatment outcomes, so it provides no evidence on whether remdesivir is effective against COVID-19.

This document is an epidemiological analysis of pediatric COVID-19 cases using crowdsourced data. It reports case counts, sex distribution, reporting delays, and symptoms. It does not mention remdesivir or any treatment and has no information on antiviral efficacy, so it is not relevant to the research question.

This is a pharmacokinetic case report of two critically ill COVID-19 patients who recovered after receiving remdesivir. It measures drug and metabolite (GS-441524) concentrations in plasma, bronchoalveolar aspirate, and CSF. It does not assess clinical efficacy: there is no comparator group, no clinical outcome analysis, and the recovery of the two patients cannot be attributed to the drug. The finding that plasma concentrations exceeded in vitro EC50 values and the low lung penetration of GS-441524 offer indirect, mechanistic context for efficacy. However, the document does not answer whether remdesivir is effective, so it is only marginally relevant.

This is a primer for cardiovascular and cardio-oncology clinicians on COVID-19 clinical trials and their biological rationale. The abstract only alludes to repurposed drugs, such as those that failed in Ebola patients (remdesivir is one such drug, though it is not named), and it names no specific agent. It reports no efficacy data and draws no conclusions about whether remdesivir works for COVID-19. It is therefore only tangentially relevant to the question.

This preclinical study tests remdesivir in SARS-CoV-2-infected rhesus macaques. Early treatment led to no respiratory disease signs, fewer pulmonary infiltrates, lower lung viral loads, and less lung damage. This is strong in vivo evidence of efficacy and supports early use in patients. It is animal data, not human clinical trial evidence, and the model does not capture severe COVID-19. Upper respiratory tract shedding was also not reduced. It therefore supports the question but does not answer it directly for human patients.

This is the Grein et al. compassionate-use cohort study of remdesivir in 53 patients with severe COVID-19. It is directly on topic, since it reports clinical outcomes with remdesivir: 68% improved in oxygen-support class, 47% were discharged, and 13% died. It cannot show effectiveness, though. It has no control group, a small sample, heterogeneous follow-up, and Gilead funding, and the authors say efficacy needs randomized, placebo-controlled trials. It offers useful preliminary, hypothesis-generating data but no strong evidence on whether remdesivir is effective.

The document is a pilot study on predicting hand-washing intentions with a web-based intervention to reduce respiratory infection transmission, based on behavioral theories (theory of planned behaviour, protection motivation theory). It does not compare coronavirus with seasonal flu in terms of virology, clinical features, transmissibility, severity, or epidemiology. Pandemic flu is mentioned only as a context for the behavioral intervention, and coronavirus is not discussed. It offers no information that answers the research question.

The abstract covers COVID-19 epidemiology, the causative virus (SARS-CoV-2) and its taxonomic similarity to SARS-CoV, the clinical spectrum (mild flu-like symptoms through pneumonia and ARDS), and respiratory and ventilator management. It never compares COVID-19 with seasonal influenza. It mentions only that mild cases can resemble flu, and says nothing on transmissibility, mortality, pathophysiology, or other key differences. Its relevance to the question is marginal and indirect.

The abstract is a general overview of COVID-19 covering its origin, spread, symptoms, prevention, management, treatment, and social impact. It mentions that patients show 'flu-like symptoms' but never compares SARS-CoV-2 with seasonal influenza in transmissibility, severity, mortality, pathogenesis, or clinical course. It therefore gives only background on COVID-19, not the comparison the question asks for. Its treatment recommendations (hydroxychloroquine, azithromycin, Unani therapy) are also weakly supported and add nothing to the comparison.

The document is a review of inhaled biguanides and mTOR inhibition as a possible treatment for influenza and coronavirus. It does not compare the two diseases in terms of transmission, clinical features, severity, or pathogenesis. It touches on both viruses and mentions that COVID-19 spreads by droplets and that PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling is involved in MERS-CoV infection. These points are only tangentially relevant to how coronavirus differs from seasonal flu. The abstract's focus is therapeutic, not comparative, so it offers little direct information for answering the question.

The question asks how coronavirus (COVID-19) differs from seasonal flu, which would call for comparisons of transmissibility, severity, symptoms, mortality, or pathogenesis. This paper does not make that comparison. It proposes that pollen explains the seasonality of flu-like epidemics, COVID-19 included, and treats the two as following a common seasonal pattern, so it speaks more to their similarities than to their differences. It touches on seasonality, one aspect of how the diseases behave, and it uses only the broad category of flu-like illness rather than distinguishing influenza from COVID-19. It is also limited to one country, and the correlations are modest (r = -0.38 and -0.48). The document is only tangentially relevant.

The question is ambiguous. It most likely refers to SARS-CoV-2/COVID-19, but this document studies seasonal human coronaviruses (OC43, NL63, HKU1, 229E), not SARS-CoV-2. It does compare clinical features of seasonal HCoV patients with influenza patients: fever and malaise were less frequent, while sore throat, dyspnoea, rhinorrhoea and conjunctivitis were more associated with HCoV. It also describes seasonality, age distribution and detection rates. This gives useful related information on how coronaviruses differ from flu. It does not address SARS-CoV-2 directly, which limits how well it answers the question, and the evidence is from a modest sentinel sample in a single region.

The abstract directly addresses the question. It analyzes 120 SARS-CoV-2 genomes and reports the co-circulation of two genetic subgroups, defined by distinct SNP markers, that can be used to trace spread across regions. This supports the existence of subtypes. It does not name or characterize the subgroups in the abstract (for example as L/S types or clades), so the answer to 'what are they' is incomplete. Much of the rest of the abstract covers recombination and the spike cleavage site insertion, which is only tangential to the question.

The document concerns co-infection of human metapneumovirus with SARS-CoV (the 2003 SARS outbreak) in Hong Kong. It does not address SARS-CoV-2 or its subtypes, lineages, or clades. Mentioning SARS-associated coronavirus is only a superficial topical overlap, and the paper has no information relevant to SARS-CoV-2 classification or variants.

The document is about a deep-learning tool that classifies coronavirus genomes at the species or family level (Alpha-CoV, Beta-CoV, MERS, SARS-CoV-1, SARS-CoV-2, bronchitis-CoV). It mentions the emergence of SARS-CoV-2 variants as a problem, but it does not identify or describe any SARS-CoV-2 subtypes, clades, lineages, or variants. It therefore does not answer the question and is only tangentially relevant, through its genome classification and passing reference to variant emergence.

The document characterizes accessory ORFs (7b, 9b, 9c, 3b, 10) in SARS-CoV-2 and related coronavirus genomes using a computational tool based on X circular code motifs. It does not address SARS-CoV-2 subtypes, lineages, clades, or variants. Comparisons with SARS-CoV and bat, civet and pangolin viruses concern related species, not subtypes of SARS-CoV-2. It therefore offers essentially no information for answering the question.

The abstract directly addresses SARS-CoV-2 genomic diversity and phylogenetic clades. It names the dominant clades by defining mutations (ORF8-L84S, ORF3a-G251V, S-D614G), describes a new clade with ORF1ab-V378I, and reports a novel ORF8-deletion mutant. This provides substantial evidence that SARS-CoV-2 has subtypes or clades and identifies several of them. It is a regional surveillance study, not a comprehensive classification of all subtypes, and it does not use standardized nomenclature such as GISAID, Nextstrain or Pango. That keeps it from the top score.

The document directly answers the research question. It proposes subdividing the global SARS-CoV-2 population into sixteen well-defined subtypes, six of which are predominant (as the title says). The subtypes are defined by widely shared polymorphisms in nsp3, nsp4, nsp6, nsp12, nsp13, nsp14, spike, nucleocapsid and ORF8. The abstract also notes amino acid replacements with possible phenotypic implications and discusses the founder effect and relevance to vaccine and drug trials. It does not list the individual subtype names or defining mutations, and the title and abstract differ on the count (six major vs. sixteen total). Even so, it clearly confirms that subtypes exist and describes how they were defined.

The abstract gives a general overview of nonclinical safety assessment and toxicity testing for prophylactic vaccines. It does not mention Covid-19, SARS-CoV-2, or any specific vaccine candidates under testing. It offers no information that could answer the research question.

The document evaluates remdesivir, an antiviral drug, as a COVID-19 treatment. It does not discuss vaccine candidates or vaccine trials. The only overlap is the general topic of COVID-19, plus a brief mention of immunogenicity in the context of coronavirus structure and pathogenesis, which does not address the research question.

The paper describes an in silico (immunoinformatics) design of a multi-peptide vaccine candidate for COVID-19 from the Spike and Nucleocapsid proteins. It names specific epitopes and predicts binding affinity, non-toxicity and non-allergenicity, so it does identify a vaccine candidate. However, the candidate is purely computational and has not been tested experimentally, in animals or in humans. The question asks which candidates are 'being tested', so the document is only moderately relevant. It adds to the picture of candidate approaches (peptide-based, epitope-focused) but gives no evidence from actual testing.

This review covers immune responses, diagnostics, and therapeutic strategies for COVID-19. Its only link to the research question is a mention that it summarizes the 'current status of various therapeutic strategies, including vaccination.' The abstract names no specific vaccine candidates, platforms, or trial information, so it does not directly answer the question. The full text might discuss vaccines, but the abstract suggests only marginal relevance.

The document describes a specific multi-epitope vaccine candidate for SARS-CoV-2, designed from spike glycoprotein B- and T-cell epitopes with a 50S ribosomal protein adjuvant. It was evaluated only in silico, using antigenicity and allergenicity prediction, TLR-3 docking, MD simulation and immune simulation. It does identify a vaccine candidate, so it is on topic. However, the candidate has not been tested experimentally or clinically, so it does not reflect candidates actually in testing. It also does not survey the wider vaccine landscape. That makes it moderately relevant: it fits a loose reading of 'being tested' (computational testing) but not a strict one.

The document describes a specific multi-epitope peptide vaccine candidate for SARS-CoV-2 (Spike, Nucleocapsid, Membrane, Envelope epitopes with flagellin, HP-91 and beta defensin 3 adjuvants). It therefore speaks to the question of what vaccine candidates exist. However, the work is purely in silico (immunoinformatics, docking, in silico cloning). The candidate has not been tested in vitro, in animals or in humans, so it is not a candidate being tested in the clinical or experimental sense. It is moderately relevant, as an example of a computationally designed candidate rather than strong evidence of candidates under active testing.

The research question asks about longer-term complications in people who have recovered from COVID-19 (e.g., post-COVID sequelae). This document is a systematic review of mental health impacts on healthcare workers who provided care during viral epidemic outbreaks, mostly SARS. It does not study COVID-19 patients or survivors and gives no data on their recovery or long-term complications. The only overlap is that it mentions long-lasting mental health effects in HCWs, which is a different population and a different exposure (working through an outbreak, not having the illness). It is not relevant to the question.

The review addresses the psychological and mental health impact of the COVID-19 pandemic (stress, anxiety, depression, quarantine effects) in the general population. It does not focus on people who recovered from COVID-19 or on longer-term post-infection sequelae, so it only partly overlaps with the question. Mental health consequences are a possible long-term complication, but the abstract is about pandemic-related distress, not complications of recovered patients, which makes it marginally relevant.

The review addresses delirium as an acute neuropsychiatric complication of COVID-19, especially in older adults, and covers prevention and management. It does not examine longer-term sequelae in people who have recovered, such as post-acute or persistent outcomes. Delirium during acute illness is only tangentially related to the question, and the abstract gives no follow-up or post-recovery data. It would offer some context on neurological complications but does not answer the question.

The document concerns dental practice and the risk of cross-infection. It suggests that the recommended 14-day postponement of dental treatment after symptom onset may be too short because of possible COVID-19 reactivation or prolonged infectivity. This touches on persistence or recurrence of infection after apparent recovery, which is loosely related to post-recovery outcomes. However, the abstract does not describe longer-term complications such as organ damage, long COVID symptoms, or sequelae. It is therefore only marginally relevant to the research question.

This position statement is about managing heart failure during COVID-19. It notes that myocardial injury can lead to cardiovascular complications including HF, but it focuses mainly on acute management, continuation of guideline-directed therapy, and protecting health care workers. It says outright that long-term cardiovascular effects of COVID-19 are not yet known, so it offers no evidence on longer-term complications in people who have recovered. It is only marginally relevant.

This case report describes the acute management of severe COVID-19 pneumonia in a liver transplant recipient, including temporary immunosuppression withdrawal and low-dose corticosteroids, with recovery. It does not report on longer-term complications or sequelae after recovery, and no follow-up data on post-COVID outcomes are given. It does not address the research question.

This scoping review covers search queries and social media for infectious disease surveillance (mostly influenza and foodborne illness) from 2002-2011. It predates COVID-19 and does not mention COVID-19 or any public datasets related to it, so it does not address the research question.

This is a narrative review of COVID-19 in pregnancy and its implications for assisted reproductive treatments. It does not describe, release, or catalog any public dataset related to COVID-19. It summarizes clinical and epidemiological findings and reproductive society recommendations, so it does not address the question about new public datasets.

The paper is an exploratory analysis of COVID-19 correlates and spatial patterns in sub-Saharan Africa using machine learning (Lasso) and Empirical Bayesian Kriging. It uses existing public data (Johns Hopkins University time series) merged with socio-demographic and health survey data, but it does not present or release a new public dataset. Its relevance to the question is marginal: it shows an example of using public COVID-19 data and mentions the merged data sources, but it does not describe a newly available dataset.

This is a general overview of NCBI database resources (GenBank, PubMed, GEO, SRA and others). It dates from before COVID-19 (it lists HIV-1 resources and UniGene and never mentions SARS-CoV-2), so it describes no new COVID-19 datasets. Some of the listed repositories, such as GenBank, SRA, and PMC, have since hosted COVID-19 data. The abstract itself does not address the question, so the relevance is only tangential.

The document describes the creation and release of a new, open, curated dataset (CAN-NPI v1.0) of 1640 Canadian non-pharmaceutical interventions for COVID-19. It gives the dataset's scope, variables (timing, location, intervention type, target population), and update plans, and it notes how the data can be linked to other sources. This directly answers the question about new public COVID-19 datasets.

The document describes COVID19-Tracker, a Shiny web app that automatically collects and visualizes daily COVID-19 case and mortality data for Spain from February 24, 2020 onward. It is a tool for analysis (trend projections, case fatality rate, lockdown effects), not a new public dataset in itself. It is related to the question because it aggregates and presents publicly available COVID-19 data, but the abstract does not say it releases a new dataset or give details on data availability. It is moderately relevant, mainly as a data-access and analysis resource rather than a dataset publication.

The document reviews the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 RNA replication machinery (RdRp, Nsp8, Nsp10, proofreading and capping enzymes), not the spike protein. It gives no information on spike structure, so it does not address the research question. Its only link is that it covers SARS-CoV-2 protein structures in general.

The document models the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 3C-like protease (3CLpro, a main protease), not the spike protein. It covers virtual drug screening and repurposing candidates such as ledipasvir and velpatasvir. It gives no information on spike protein structure, so it is not relevant to the research question, apart from the general topic of SARS-CoV-2 protein structure.

The paper uses immunoinformatics to identify B and T cell epitopes on the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein and to build a multi-epitope vaccine construct. It does not determine or describe the spike's protein structure, such as its domain architecture, S1/S2 organization, trimeric assembly, or conformational states. The abstract only notes the spike's role in attachment, fusion, and entry. Its structural content concerns the designed vaccine construct and its docking and molecular dynamics with TLR3, not the spike itself. It is therefore only tangentially related to the question.

The abstract is about ACE2 as the entry receptor for SARS-CoV-2, its role in the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and acute lung injury, and the use of ACEIs/ARBs. It does not describe the structure of the spike protein (domains, RBD, trimer conformation, S1/S2). It mentions only that SARS-CoV-2 binds ACE2 with high affinity, which is tangential context for spike-receptor interaction. It does not answer the question about spike protein structure.

The document is about generating polyclonal antibodies against the SARS-CoV (the 2003 virus, not SARS-CoV-2) spike and nucleocapsid proteins for diagnostic detection. It does not describe the structure of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (e.g., domains, trimer architecture, RBD conformations, cryo-EM data). Its only link to the question is that it mentions a spike protein of a related coronavirus, so it is not relevant to the structural question.

The study builds 3D structural models of the SARS-CoV-2 spike glycoprotein, including its glycan shield, from reported 3D structures and glycomics data. It uses molecular dynamics simulation to analyze surface shielding, which is a structural property of the spike. It also reports quantitative findings: glycans account for 17% of molecular weight but shield 42% of the surface, and the ACE2 receptor binding domain is the exception. It does not describe the core protein architecture (S1/S2 subunits, RBD, trimer organization, prefusion conformation) as its main focus, so it is not a direct answer. It still gives substantial structural information, especially on glycosylation and its effects on antibody accessibility.

The study uses network-based modeling of HCoV–host interactomes and compares the 3D structure of the SARS-CoV-2 S-glycoprotein with those of SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV and HCoV-229E. It does not perform a phylogenetic analysis of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. The only overlap is an incidental comparison of S-glycoprotein amino acid sequences and structures, which found SARS-CoV closest to SARS-CoV-2. That hints at relatedness but is not a phylogenetic result, so the document is only marginally relevant.

The research question concerns phylogenetic analysis of the SARS-CoV-2 genome sequence. This document analyzes partial spike gene sequences of human coronavirus OC43 (HCoV-OC43) in coastal Kenya, 2015–16. It is a different virus, and the study predates SARS-CoV-2. It uses phylogenetics on a coronavirus, but its findings (genotypes G and H, clade co-circulation, global spread) say nothing about SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny. It is only tangentially related by methodology and virus family, so it is not relevant.

The abstract reports a phylogenetic analysis of 12 full SARS-CoV-2 genomes from Taiwan. The sequences fell into different clades, so no major strain was circulating locally. It also reports an ORF8 deletion in one isolate and only a 4-nucleotide difference among genomes from a cluster. These are direct phylogenetic results, which answers the question well. The scope is limited to Taiwanese isolates and the sample is small, so the findings are not a general account of SARS-CoV-2 phylogeny.

This paper directly reports population genetic and phylogenetic-type analyses of SARS-CoV-2 genome sequences. It finds 4% nucleotide divergence from bat RaTG13 but 17% at neutral sites, which suggests a larger divergence than previously estimated. Across 103 genomes, the viruses fall into two major types (L and S) defined by two linked SNPs, with S as the ancestral type. It also gives their relative frequencies and how these changed over time. This addresses the question of what genome-sequence phylogenetic analysis shows about SARS-CoV-2 origin and evolution. The L/S lineage interpretation is based on limited early data and was later criticized, which slightly reduces the strength of evidence, but the paper is still directly on topic.

The abstract reports a phylogenetic-type result: the SARS-CoV-2 genome sequenced from raw wastewater belonged to the strain most widespread in Europe and was similar to another strain found in the same region. This addresses the question directly, but only in one sentence. It gives no detail on the phylogenetic method, clade or lineage designation, or tree topology. The rest of the paper covers wastewater and river detection and infectivity, which is not what the question asks about. It is therefore moderately relevant.

The abstract directly reports a phylogenetic result: the phylogenetic tree showed SARS-CoV-2 was 96.2% identical to bat β-coronaviruses from lineage B. This answers the question about the outcome of phylogenetic analysis of the SARS-CoV-2 genome. The document is a review, so it reports the finding secondhand and gives few details on methods, on the specific bat virus (e.g., RaTG13), or on the relationship to SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV. Most of the abstract covers pathogenesis, ACE2 receptor use, and therapy options, which are outside the question. It earns a 4 rather than a 5 because the phylogenetic content is a single sentence from a secondary source.

The document concerns multiple sclerosis, specifically immune complexes of myelin basic protein, anti-MBP antibodies, and complement, and how they affect CD4+ T-cell and cytokine responses. It does not mention COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, or the inflammatory pathogenesis of viral infection. The shared themes of cytokines (TNF-α, IFN-γ, IL-10) and complement are too generic to inform the mechanism of inflammation in COVID-19.

The document is a general chapter on descriptive statistics (histograms, measures of central tendency, probability, normal distribution). It says nothing about COVID-19, inflammation, or disease pathogenesis, so it has no bearing on the research question.

The document is a review of saliva as a route of SARS-CoV-2 transmission (droplets and aerosols) and as a non-invasive diagnostic and immune-surveillance tool. It does not address the mechanisms of the inflammatory response (e.g., cytokine storm, innate or adaptive immune dysregulation) or the pathogenesis of COVID-19. Its only link to the question is background on viral detection and immune status monitoring, so it is essentially not relevant.

This is a retrospective clinical cohort of multiple myeloma patients with COVID-19. It was not designed to study the mechanism of the inflammatory response or the pathogenesis of COVID-19. It does report that elevated inflammatory markers (CRP, ferritin, D-dimer) and severe hypogammaglobulinemia were associated with higher mortality. It also reports that 96% of patients developed antibodies to SARS-CoV-2, and it gives viral PCR persistence data. These findings touch on the inflammatory response and the humoral response only in an association-based way within a specific immunocompromised population. They offer little mechanistic insight into general COVID-19 pathogenesis, so the paper is marginally relevant.

The title promises a pathogenesis comparison, but the abstract only partly covers it. It gives the phylogenetic origin of SARS-CoV-2, ACE2 receptor use for cell entry, and the lung alveoli and small intestine as likely target tissues, which bear on the early stages of pathogenesis. It says nothing about the inflammatory response, such as cytokine storm, immune cell activation, or host immune dysregulation, and the stated focus is mainly on therapy options borrowed from SARS and MERS. It is useful background on pathogenesis but does not directly answer the question about inflammatory mechanisms.

This retrospective cohort study (45 severe and 12 non-severe patients) describes changes in peripheral blood inflammatory cells in COVID-19: lymphopenia, eosinopenia, basopenia, neutrophilia, and reduced T and NK cell counts in patients with poor outcomes. These findings bear on the immune dysregulation and inflammatory cell dynamics of COVID-19 pathogenesis, and they suggest that cellular immunity is involved in disease progression. However, the study is observational and prognostic. It does not examine molecular or cellular mechanisms such as cytokine storm, innate immune signaling, or viral-host interactions, so it does not directly answer the question about the mechanism of the inflammatory response. It offers moderate supporting information rather than a mechanistic explanation.

The abstract gives a general overview of infectious disease threats: emerging infections, antimicrobial resistance, climate change, terrorism, pandemics, and surveillance. It does not mention COVID-19, cytokine storm syndrome, or any immunopathological mechanism, so it does not help answer the question.

The document is a review of regulatory T cells in the pathogenesis and biological therapy of multiple sclerosis. It does not mention COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, or cytokine storm syndrome. Its discussion of T cell subsets (TH1, TH17, Tregs) and immunotherapies is only loosely connected to general immunology and does not address the mechanism of cytokine storm in COVID-19. It is not relevant to the research question.

The abstract addresses COVID-19 cytokine storm syndrome (CSS) and ARDS mechanisms directly. It describes a murine model induced by SARS-CoV-2 components and tests which cytokines and signaling pathways drive CSS. Blocking IL-1α, IL-6, TNFα and GM-CSF, or inhibiting p38, JAK, ERK and MPO, partially relieved CSS and neutrophilic alveolitis, which implicates these mediators and pathways. The evidence comes from an animal model using viral components rather than live virus, and the abstract gives no detailed mechanistic account. It therefore supports the mechanism question substantially but does not answer it fully.

The document is a case report on a cutaneous adverse reaction (toxic erythema) and eosinophilia after tocilizumab in a COVID-19 patient. The abstract only briefly notes that SARS-CoV-2 ssRNA is recognized by PRRs, which trigger NF-kB and IRFs. That is a minimal, introductory nod to the start of the inflammatory cascade. It does not describe the mechanism of cytokine storm syndrome (IL-6, TNF, IL-1 signaling, hyperinflammation, etc.), so it is only marginally relevant.

This is a hypothesis paper proposing (18)F-Fluorocholine PET/CT to image macrophage activity in COVID-19 pneumonia. It does not directly investigate the mechanism of cytokine storm syndrome, and it presents no experimental evidence. It does contain mechanism-relevant content: macrophages and macrophage activation syndrome (MAS) are described as central to the abnormal hyper-inflammatory response, with a link to multisystemic coagulopathy. It also suggests that cytokine storm/MAS increases choline consumption for phosphatidylcholine synthesis, which supports phagocytosis and secretory functions. This gives useful but limited and mostly speculative context on the mechanism, and the paper's main focus is diagnostic imaging.

This review argues that monocytes are principal players in the cytokine storm and related pathologies of severe COVID-19. It also links age-related changes in monocyte function and phenotype to a possible mechanism for worse outcomes in older adults, which bears directly on the mechanism question. It is a narrative review with a hypothesis-driven focus on monocytes and aging, not a comprehensive account of cytokine storm mechanisms (for example, it does not detail IL-6, IFN, or NF-κB signaling pathways). It also acknowledges that the evidence is largely observational and that experimental studies are still needed. It is therefore highly relevant but not a complete answer.

The document studies mutations (deletions) in the 3c and 7b genes of feline coronavirus in cats with feline infectious peritonitis. It does not examine the SARS-CoV-2 genome, its mutations, or how often they occur. The shared interest in coronavirus mutations is only a loose thematic link, and the findings cannot answer the research question.

The paper uses ribosome profiling to map the SARS-CoV-2 coding regions. It identifies 23 novel ORFs and a CUG initiation codon in the 5'UTR. It does not report mutations in the viral genome, their frequency, or variant or evolutionary analyses. Its subject is the genome's coding capacity and translation, not mutation observation or mutation rates, so it is essentially unrelated to the research question.

The paper identifies potential G-quadruplexes in the SARS-CoV-2 genome and analyzes the SUD-like domain. It is only marginally relevant to the question about observed mutations and their frequency. It does report that the SUD-like sequence is almost conserved across 16,466 SARS-CoV-2 samples, and that G-quartets in related bat and pangolin coronaviruses are under selective constraint. These are indirect statements about sequence variation (conservation) in specific regions. The abstract gives no catalog of observed mutations across the genome and no mutation frequencies or rates, so it does not directly answer the question.

This review covers the mechanisms of coronavirus cell entry mediated by the spike protein: receptor binding, low pH, proteolytic activation, and conformational changes. It does not discuss observed mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 genome or their frequency or mutation rates. The abstract mentions features related to tropism and host interspecies transmission, but only in general terms and without any mutation data. It is therefore essentially not relevant to the research question.

The abstract is about computationally identifying conserved, high free energy sites in the spike glycoproteins of all human coronaviruses, as possible targets for interference. It does not report observed SARS-CoV-2 mutations or how often they occur. The only link is that the sites are conserved across hCoVs and so may stay functional despite 'inevitable viral mutation'. That is a tangential connection to mutation and gives no data on mutation types or frequencies.

The abstract directly addresses both parts of the question. It identifies 37 single-nucleotide substitutions occurring in more than 1% of 480 full-length SARS-CoV-2 genomes, which answers what mutations were observed and how often. It also characterizes the mutation types (mostly C to T and G to A), mutation hotspots (C/Gs with an upstream TTT motif), co-occurring mutations, and three mutually exclusive lineages (A1, B1, C1) that account for about three quarters of the genomes. The sample is limited to early-pandemic sequences, but the study is a comprehensive mutation landscape analysis with explicit frequency thresholds.

This is a protocol for a systematic review of health promotion interventions for African Americans in barbershops and hair salons, targeting obesity-related chronic disease (cardiovascular disease, cancer, type 2 diabetes). It does not mention COVID-19 or its impacts, and it offers no comparison with the rest of the U.S. population. Its only link to the question is the general topic of health disparities among African Americans, so it is not relevant.

This is an ecological study of smoking prevalence and COVID-19 occurrence and mortality across 38 European nations. It does not examine African-Americans, racial or ethnic disparities, or any comparison with the rest of the U.S. population. Its setting (Europe), population level and focus (smoking) do not address the research question.

This scoping review covers COVID-19 infections and deaths among healthcare workers worldwide, including breakdowns by gender, profession, age, and region. It does not examine African-Americans, racial or ethnic disparities, or any comparison with the rest of the U.S. population. The only mention of Africa concerns low reported rates on the continent, which is unrelated to the experience of African-Americans in the U.S. The document does not address the research question.

The document addresses COVID-19 vulnerability among refugees and migrant populations in the Americas (Central American migrants, Venezuelans, Haitians in the Dominican Republic). It does not discuss African-Americans or compare their COVID-19 outcomes with the broader U.S. population. The only loose connection is the shared topic of health disparities in vulnerable groups, which does not address the research question.

The perspective piece looks at COVID-19 in Metropolitan Detroit, where African American and low-income communities were disproportionately affected. It discusses excess exposure, higher mortality, and reduced access to health-protective resources, and it frames these as products of structural drivers (environment, occupation, housing). It also considers lasting life-course impacts for health equity. This speaks directly to how COVID-19 impacts on African Americans differ from those on the rest of the U.S. population, and it explains why. It is a perspective rather than a primary empirical study, and it focuses on one metropolitan area. It also devotes part of its content to recommendations for health educators, so it is highly relevant but not a definitive source of quantified disparities.

The document's title and framing address a racial disparity in COVID-19 infection risk among African American children. This is a specific way the pandemic's impact on African Americans differs from the rest of the U.S. population. The abstract also cites evidence of higher COVID-19 rates and fatality among African American adults. However, the provided text is mostly background and a statement of the knowledge gap. It reports no actual data or quantitative findings, so the evidence it offers is limited. It is highly relevant in topic but only moderately strong in evidence.

This document is a general book chapter on nutrition and lung disease, covering alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, asthma, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The abstract does not mention COVID-19 or vitamin D, and it offers no evidence on vitamin D for COVID-19 prevention or treatment. It is not relevant to the research question.

This RCT (pre-COVID, 2010-2011) tested vitamin D3 supplementation for preventing upper respiratory tract infections in 600 university students. It does not study COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2. It is indirectly relevant because it offers randomized evidence that vitamin D may reduce laboratory-confirmed viral respiratory infections and viral load, which supports the biological plausibility of a preventive effect against respiratory viruses. The primary outcome of clinical URTI was not statistically significant (RR 0.79, p=0.09). The pathogens were general URTI viruses, not coronaviruses specifically, and the study says nothing about treating COVID-19. It is therefore only moderately relevant as indirect, extrapolated evidence.

This is a general review of COVID-19 transmission, prevention, and therapeutic options. The abstract never mentions vitamin D, so it provides no direct evidence on the research question. The full text might discuss vitamin D among the therapeutic or preventive options, but the abstract gives no indication of that. It is only tangentially relevant, through its broad coverage of prevention and treatment.

This review mentions vitamin D only in passing, as part of sunlight-induced inherent immunity, and does not directly evaluate vitamin D for COVID-19 prevention or treatment. Its main focus is meteorological factors (temperature, humidity, sun exposure) and general immunity in relation to COVID-19 prevalence in South East Asia. Any link to vitamin D is indirect and speculative. The abstract gives no vitamin D-specific data such as serum levels, supplementation, or clinical outcomes. It is therefore only marginally relevant.

This is a nutritional care protocol for non-critically ill hospitalized COVID-19 patients. Vitamin D is only a minor component: cholecalciferol is given when 25-hydroxyvitamin D deficiency is detected, as part of a broader package of supplements. The document presents no data on vitamin D's effect on COVID-19 prevention or treatment outcomes and does not assess vitamin D efficacy. It is marginally relevant because it mentions vitamin D supplementation in COVID-19 management, but it does not answer the research question.

This is a rheumatology-focused review of COVID-19 pathogenesis and potential therapies (hydroxychloroquine, antivirals, immunosuppression, ACE2 considerations, vaccines). The abstract never mentions vitamin D, either for prevention or for treatment, so it provides no evidence on the research question.

This is an editorial introduction to a special issue on COVID-19's effects on business and research (tourism, retail, higher education, consumer behavior, ethics, employees, leadership). It does not discuss violence, violent crime, domestic violence, or related public safety outcomes. The only overlap is the general statement that society was affected, which gives no information on the research question.

The document evaluates PCR/ESI-MS and virus microarray technologies for detecting retroviruses, such as XMRV, in biological products and cell lines. It does not address COVID-19, violence, or violent crime, so it has no relevance to the research question.

The abstract addresses a pandemic-related aspect of violence: increased firearm purchases in the US during COVID-19, driven by fear and anxiety, and the strain that gun violence victims place on ICU resources. This is relevant to the question's theme of violence and the pandemic. However, it is a commentary-style piece that provides no direct data on violent crime rates, such as homicides, assaults, or domestic violence. It only implies a potential rise in gun violence through increased gun ownership, so it is moderately relevant rather than directly answering the question.

This review covers the psychosocial and mental health effects of COVID-19, including panic, anxiety, PTSD, and burnout. Its only link to the research question is a brief mention of outbursts of racism, stigmatization, and xenophobia against particular communities, which touches on social hostility. It does not examine violence in society, violent crime, domestic violence, or crime statistics, so it is only marginally relevant.

The document is an essay on COVID-19 social isolation, intensive internet use among children and adolescents, and the risk of self-inflicted violence (self-harm challenges, suicidal ideation). The research question is about violence in society and violent crimes. Self-directed violence is a form of violence and the paper links it to the pandemic, so it is loosely related. However, it does not address interpersonal violence, domestic violence, or violent crime, and it provides no empirical data. It is a conceptual discussion rather than strong evidence. Its relevance is therefore marginal.

The paper addresses how COVID-19 affected victimization, but its main focus is fraud (a non-violent crime) among adults 50 and over. It also covers parent abuse, partner violence, and patient abuse, which are forms of violence, but only briefly, and the empirical evidence is mostly FTC fraud data from early 2020. It is moderately relevant: it shows the pandemic's impact on crime and touches on interpersonal violence in a specific population, but it does not directly or comprehensively answer the question about violence and violent crime in society.

The document describes enhanced Traffic Control Bundling, a hospital-based infection control strategy, and mentions face masks only as one component (required for all visitors entering hospitals). It does not isolate or quantify the effect of masks on COVID-19 transmission. Taiwan's success is attributed to the whole bundle, which includes quarantine wards, hand disinfection, PPE and zoning, so the evidence for mask impact is indirect and confounded. It is marginally relevant because masks are part of the intervention, but it does not answer the question.

This is a cross-sectional survey of psychological impact, anxiety, depression and stress in the Chinese public early in the COVID-19 outbreak. Mask wearing appears only as a precautionary measure associated with lower psychological distress. The study does not measure whether masks prevent transmission or infection, so it does not address the research question about the effectiveness of masks in limiting COVID-19 spread.

This is a general mini-review of COVID-19 epidemiology, clinical features, and prevention. It mentions masks only in passing, as one of several recommended preventive measures (alongside hand washing, staying home, avoiding public contact, and quarantine). It presents no data, effect estimates, or analysis of how much masks reduce transmission, so it does not address the question of impact. It is only marginally relevant.

The document covers French guidelines for the rational use of surgical and FFP masks by healthcare workers during COVID-19, with a focus on indications and supply management. It does not quantify how much masks prevent SARS-CoV-2 transmission, and it presents no effectiveness data. It relates to mask use in the pandemic, so it is tangentially relevant, but it does not answer the question about impact on spread.

The study directly estimates the impact of mask recommendations on COVID-19 spread. It uses a causal, counterfactual framework based on Rt changes and reports a quantified effect: about 170,000 fewer cases (95% CI 160,000 to 180,000) in Connecticut, Massachusetts, and New York State. This answers 'how much impact' with a specific figure. The evidence is observational and model-based, and it covers only a limited region. It also measures the effect of a recommendation to wear masks, not mask efficacy itself, which stops it short of a perfect match. Even so, it addresses the question very closely.

This is the Leung et al. (Nature Medicine, 2020) study of exhaled breath. It shows surgical masks significantly reduced detection of seasonal coronavirus RNA in aerosols and influenza RNA in droplets, with a trend toward reduced coronavirus RNA in droplets. It is highly relevant mechanistic and source-control evidence that masks can block viral shedding from symptomatic people. However, it studied seasonal coronaviruses (not SARS-CoV-2), measured viral RNA in exhaled breath rather than actual transmission or infection outcomes, and had a small sample size. It therefore supports mask efficacy for COVID-19 by analogy but does not directly quantify their impact on SARS-CoV-2 spread.

The document is a virology and wildlife surveillance study of coronavirus diversity and prevalence in Australasian bats. It makes no mention of COVID-19, the pandemic, or mental health outcomes, so it is not relevant to the research question.

The study examines fatalism, meaning the association of coronavirus with death, as a predictor of reluctance to follow preventative behaviors such as social distancing and handwashing. It is set in the pandemic and touches on psychological attitudes. However, it does not measure mental health outcomes such as anxiety, depression, distress, or wellbeing, and it does not assess how the pandemic affected mental health. Its focus is on health behavior and public health messaging. The relevance to the research question is therefore marginal and tangential, limited to the loosely psychological construct of fatalism.

This Lancet Psychiatry position paper (Holmes et al., 2020) addresses the mental health impact of COVID-19 and covers psychological, social, and neuroscientific effects, vulnerable groups, and media exposure. It is highly relevant to the topic. However, it is a priority-setting and call-to-action paper built on expert panel input and public surveys from the first weeks of the UK pandemic, not an empirical study that measures the impact. It therefore gives substantial context and framing but not strong direct evidence of how mental health was affected, which keeps it from the top score.

This case report addresses the mental health impact of COVID-19, specifically psychotic relapse triggered by quarantine and confinement in a vulnerable patient with a pre-existing psychotic disorder. It is topically on point and supports the idea that pandemic-related stress can worsen existing mental illness. It also raises practical implications, such as support programs and telemedicine. However, a single case report is weak evidence. It covers only one subpopulation and cannot show the broader prevalence or magnitude of pandemic effects on mental health. The abstract offers mostly background framing and little data. This makes it moderately relevant.

This study directly addresses the research question. It is a national cross-sectional survey (n=1515) that measured the prevalence of depressive symptoms (24.7%), anxiety symptoms (23.2%), and sleep disturbances (42.2%, with 17.4% of those reporting moderate/severe insomnia) in Italy during the COVID-19 lockdown. It also identifies risk factors (female sex, more time on the internet, peer-pressure avoidance, chronic conditions) and protective factors (older age, no work troubles, being married or cohabiting). Limitations are the cross-sectional design, the lack of a pre-pandemic baseline, and the use of brief screening tools rather than diagnostic assessment. It is still strong, specific evidence of the pandemic's mental health impact in a defined population.

This cross-sectional study directly measures the mental health impact of COVID-19, using the validated PHQ-9 and GAD-7 instruments to assess depression and anxiety. It reports prevalence (23.8% depression, 13.1% anxiety) across the general population, healthcare professionals, and university students. It also identifies risk factors (female sex, divorced status, chronic disease, high income) and vulnerable groups needing intervention. Limitations are the single-country setting (Jordan), the online survey design, the short data collection window (one week in March 2020), and the lack of a pre-pandemic baseline, so it cannot show change over time. Even so, it answers the question with relevant, specific evidence.

This is a general review of COVID-19 treatments that searched the literature up to April 15, 2020. That date is before the RECOVERY trial results on dexamethasone (June 2020), so it cannot contain the key evidence for dexamethasone. The abstract does not mention dexamethasone or corticosteroids. It might briefly cover corticosteroids as one of many candidate therapies, but the abstract gives no sign of this. It is only marginally relevant to the question.

The document is about steroidogenesis and steroid signaling transcripts in the equine placenta and endometrium during pregnancy. It does not mention dexamethasone, COVID-19, or any clinical treatment. It is not relevant to the research question.

This early-pandemic review covers NSAIDs and corticosteroids in general and never mentions dexamethasone specifically. It says there may be some evidence that corticosteroids help if given early in acute infection, but it calls this inconclusive and conflicting, and it contains no trial data such as RECOVERY. It is marginally relevant because dexamethasone is a corticosteroid, but it offers little direct or strong evidence on dexamethasone for COVID-19.

This network meta-analysis covers COVID-19 pharmacological treatments but searched only up to June 9th, 2020. That predates the RECOVERY trial dexamethasone results, which are the main evidence for dexamethasone. Dexamethasone is not assessed specifically. The only related finding is that corticosteroids as a class increased mortality in critically ill patients (GRADE moderate), based on pre-RECOVERY observational data. This is tangentially relevant and arguably misleading for the question. It is not direct evidence for dexamethasone, and it was later contradicted by randomized trials.

The document is a small case series (n=6) of corticosteroids in severe COVID-19 pneumonia with hyper-inflammation, reporting favorable outcomes such as avoiding intubation and ICU admission and resolution of ARDS. It is relevant to the broader question of steroid therapy for COVID-19. However, it does not specify dexamethasone, since the abstract refers to 'corticosteroids' generally, and the design (uncontrolled, tiny sample, before-after comparison) provides weak evidence compared with randomized trials such as RECOVERY. It offers supportive, hypothesis-generating information but does not directly or strongly answer the question about dexamethasone.

This review covers emerging pharmacological therapies for ARDS, including a general discussion of drugs under investigation for COVID-19-induced ARDS. The abstract never mentions dexamethasone or corticosteroids, and it gives no specific evidence on dexamethasone for COVID-19. Immune-modulating therapies are within its scope, so the full text may touch on corticosteroids. As written, though, the abstract offers only tangential context and no direct evidence on the question.

The abstract is a general overview of how the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic affected healthcare systems and policy responses in Italy, Austria, Germany, and the UK. It mentions the impact on paediatricians and respiratory paediatricians, but it reports no data on clinical outcomes (severity, hospitalization, mortality, long-term sequelae) for children who contract COVID-19. It is therefore only tangentially relevant and does not answer the research question.

The study focuses on mode of delivery and maternal outcomes in pregnant women with COVID-19, with only limited neonatal data. It reports that a few newborns tested positive for SARS-CoV-2 (two after breastfeeding without a mask, one after operative vaginal delivery) and suggests a low risk of intrapartum transmission. These findings relate to neonatal infection and transmission, not to the health outcomes of children who contract COVID-19. The abstract gives no clinical outcomes for the infected newborns, so it is only marginally relevant.

This study looks at the financial burden and hospitalization length for children with COVID-19 in Korea, using billing data. It reports hospitalization duration and costs by age group, which are loosely tied to disease severity and resource use. It gives no clinical outcomes such as symptoms, severe disease, ICU admission, mortality, MIS-C, or long-term sequelae, which are the core of the question. Its relevance is therefore marginal: it offers only an indirect economic and healthcare utilization perspective.

The study covers endemic human coronaviruses (OC43, NL63, HKU1, 229E) in children from 2012-2016, before SARS-CoV-2 emerged, so it does not address COVID-19. It does report pediatric outcomes (lower respiratory tract disease, oxygen need) and risk factors such as immunocompromise, young age, underlying pulmonary disease and RSV co-infection. These may give some loose context for coronavirus severity in children. However, the findings cannot be applied directly to the health outcomes of children with COVID-19, so the document is only marginally relevant.

This case series of 64 pediatric COVID-19 cases in Chicago reports outcomes directly relevant to the question. It gives hospitalization (16%), ICU admission (70% of those hospitalized), length of stay (median 4 days), symptoms associated with hospitalization (fever, dyspnea), and risk factors for severe disease (younger age, underlying comorbidities, co-infection). It also describes household transmission. Limitations are the small sample, the early-pandemic urban setting, the short follow-up, and the lack of data on long-term outcomes or mortality. These keep it from being a definitive answer, but it is highly relevant and provides substantial supporting information.

This retrospective study of 26 pediatric COVID-19 patients addresses the research question directly. It reports clinical outcomes: 9 children were asymptomatic, 11 had fever, and others had cough, rhinorrhea, diarrhea or vomiting. Chest CT showed unilateral pneumonia in 11 and no infiltration in 8. Some had lymphocytopenia or raised transaminases. No severe complications such as ARDS or acute lung injury occurred, and the authors conclude that the disease was mild with a good prognosis. The evidence is limited by the small sample size, the single-center retrospective design, the short follow-up and the lack of long-term outcome data (e.g., MIS-C, long COVID), so it is highly relevant but not definitive.

The document is about mold contamination (ERMI metric) and PM2.5 in schools with differing asthma prevalence. It does not address COVID-19, school reopening, transmission risks, or the educational, social and health benefits of in-person schooling. The only overlap is that it concerns school buildings and indoor environmental quality, which is at most a distant link to reopening safety. It provides no evidence that helps answer the research question.

The document argues for including children in SARS-CoV-2 vaccine development and notes that children likely play a role in transmission, which is loosely relevant to the risks of school reopening. It does not address school reopening, school-based transmission, educational or social benefits, or mitigation strategies. Its link to the research question is indirect: it supports the idea that vaccinating children could eventually make schools safer, and it notes that children's disease burden is probably underestimated. Overall it is only marginally relevant.

The document addresses children's outdoor recreational and physical activity during Italy's COVID-19 lockdown easing (Phase 2). It is tangentially related because it discusses the risks and benefits of children resuming some out-of-home activity with social distancing. However, it does not discuss school re-opening, in-school transmission, educational outcomes, or the specific benefits and risks of returning to classrooms. It is a recommendation or opinion piece without empirical evidence on schools, so it offers little direct help in answering the research question.

The paper uses a causal model to project COVID-19 spread in the US under lockdown and general public safety measures. It does not address school reopening, school closures, children's education or wellbeing, or transmission in school settings, so it offers nothing on the benefits and risks of reopening schools. At most it is loosely related through its discussion of lockdown and social distancing, and its projections are specific to general lockdowns.

The document is a commentary on competency-based medical education and early graduation of medical trainees to address COVID-19 workforce pressures. It does not discuss re-opening schools, transmission in school settings, child outcomes, or the educational and social benefits and risks of school re-opening. Its only link to the research question is the pandemic context, so it is not relevant.

This is a SEIR modeling paper on tailored social distancing, protection of vulnerable groups, and tracing apps. It does not address school reopening, children, or education settings. Its general discussion of trade-offs between death toll, health system overload, and epidemic duration when easing restrictions, and of group-specific measures, is loosely related to reopening decisions. It offers no school-specific benefits or risks, so it is only marginally relevant.

The document addresses inferring force of infection in wildlife populations from individual antibody kinetics (influenza A in snow geese, Yersinia pestis in coyotes). It does not study COVID-19, human convalescent immunity, T-cell responses, or protection against SARS-CoV-2 re-infection. The only overlap is the general concept of antibody dynamics, which is too tangential to inform the research question.

This review looks at how raising aerobic capacity might strengthen immune and respiratory function and lower COVID-19 risk and progression. It does not address immunity after COVID-19 recovery, such as antibody levels, T-cell responses, or protection against re-infection. Its mention of immune cells and immunoglobulins concerns exercise-related immune modulation in general, not post-infection immunity, so it is essentially unrelated to the research question.

This study looks at re-positive RT-PCR tests in discharged COVID-19 patients in Brunei. It concludes that prolonged, intermittent viral shedding is the likely cause rather than true re-infection, and it found no onward transmission to close contacts. This bears indirectly on the re-infection question, since it suggests many re-positives are not true re-infections. It measures no antibody levels or T-cell immunity, so it cannot show whether recovered individuals mount a sufficient immune response to prevent re-infection. It is therefore only marginally relevant.

This early-pandemic review discusses unanswered questions about SARS-CoV-2 host immune response and pathogenesis, including immunity in asymptomatic individuals, immune evasion in severe disease, and age/gender differences. It does not present data on antibody levels, T-cell immunity, or protection from re-infection after recovery. It gives only general background on immunology and is therefore marginally relevant. It does not answer the research question or provide evidence about re-infection protection.

This review covers the antibody response to SARS-CoV-2 mainly in the context of passive immunization (convalescent plasma, monoclonal antibodies, soluble ACE2) and vaccine design. It says neutralizing antibodies are 'likely to protect' and raises the possibility of antibody-dependent enhancement. However, it does not assess whether recovered individuals have antibody levels or T-cell immunity sufficient to prevent re-infection. It presents no data on re-infection rates, durability of immunity, or T-cell responses, so it is only tangentially relevant.

The study reports that 2 of 62 recovered medical staff (3.23%) tested PCR-positive after discharge while asymptomatic. This is loosely related to the question of re-infection or persistent viral presence after recovery. However, the abstract does not measure antibody levels or T-cell immunity, so it cannot show whether immunity is sufficient to prevent re-infection. It also does not distinguish true re-infection from prolonged viral shedding or false-negative results at discharge. The findings are tangential, and the document mainly supports the need for post-discharge surveillance.

The document describes synthetic monoclonal antibodies that bind the SARS-CoV-2 spike RBD, compete with ACE2, and neutralize the virus in Vero E6 cells, as potential immunotherapeutics. It does not address mRNA vaccines, their design, delivery, immunogenicity, or efficacy. The only overlap is the shared target (SARS-CoV-2 spike), so it is not relevant to the question.

This is a review of human and novel coronavirus infections in children, covering clinical presentation, epidemiology, MIS-C, and the effects of pandemic control measures. It does not discuss mRNA vaccines, their mechanism, development, safety, or efficacy. The only vaccine-related content is a generic statement that vaccine trials should include paediatric considerations, which tells us nothing about mRNA vaccines for SARS-CoV-2. It is essentially irrelevant to the research question.

This is a general review of COVID-19 epidemiology, diagnosis, therapeutics, and vaccine development. The abstract says global institutions and companies have begun developing vaccines, but it never mentions mRNA vaccines. The full text may include a section on mRNA vaccine candidates (such as Moderna's mRNA-1273), but the abstract gives no evidence of that. The document is only marginally relevant to the question about mRNA vaccines.

The document is about the molecular biology of coronavirus replication, specifically antileader sequences on minus-strand copies of porcine transmissible gastroenteritis coronavirus mRNAs. It says nothing about mRNA vaccines, SARS-CoV-2, vaccine design, immunogenicity, or efficacy. The word 'mRNA' here means viral subgenomic transcripts, not a vaccine platform. It is not relevant to the research question.

This is a general review of emerging SARS-CoV-2 therapies and vaccines, written around mid-2020 (about 6.5 million cases). The abstract does not mention mRNA vaccines. The full text may cover mRNA candidates such as Moderna's mRNA-1273 among the vaccines in development, but the abstract gives no evidence of this and no specific findings. It is only marginally relevant to the question about mRNA vaccines.

The document directly addresses an RNA-based vaccine for SARS-CoV-2. It describes a self-amplifying mRNA (saRNA) encoding the spike protein in a lipid nanoparticle and reports preclinical immunogenicity in mice. Findings include dose-dependent high antibody titers, neutralization of pseudo-virus and wild-type virus at levels above those in recovered COVID-19 patients, a Th1-biased response, no antibody-dependent enhancement, and strong cellular (IFN-γ) responses. This is strong preclinical evidence on design and immunogenicity of an mRNA-type vaccine. Limitations are that it is a self-amplifying platform rather than conventional mRNA, and it is mouse data without human efficacy or safety results.
